Transcript: OK, everyone, let's get started. Last week we looked at how a violin makes its sound, how the strings shake the thin wooden top and the whole body of the instrument. Today I want to tell you about an experiment that surprised a lot of musicians.

So, some of the most famous violins in the world were made in northern Italy about three hundred years ago. Today a single one of them can sell for several million dollars. That's more than most houses. And for a long time, almost everyone in classical music believed these old violins had a special sound that no modern maker could copy. People wrote whole books about the secret. Was it the wood? The varnish? Some treatment nobody remembers?

About fifteen years ago, a group of researchers decided to test that belief directly. They brought together around twenty experienced violinists and gave them six instruments to play. Three were famous old Italian violins. Three were new ones from good modern makers, some only a few years old. Here's the clever part. The players wore dark glasses, a bit like the goggles welders use, so they couldn't see which violin was which. The room was kept dim, too. The researchers even put a little perfume on each violin, so nobody could recognise the smell of old wood. In other words, it was a blind test.

The players tried the violins, compared them in pairs, and picked the one they'd most like to take home. And the result? Most of them couldn't tell old from new any better than if they'd simply guessed. The violin they liked most was a new one. And the one they liked least was one of the famous old ones.

Now, you might think those players just weren't good enough. So a few years later the team ran a second test with top concert soloists, the kind of people who've played these old instruments on stage for years. This time they played in a real concert hall, again with their eyes covered. Six of the ten chose a new violin as their favourite. Later tests with audiences found much the same thing. Listeners in the hall often preferred the new violins.

So what's going on? I think these experiments show something important about how we listen. When players know they're holding a violin worth millions, they expect it to sound wonderful, and that expectation becomes part of what they hear. Take away the name and the price, and the difference mostly disappears.

I'm not saying the old violins are bad. They're beautiful instruments, and some players will always love them. But the idea of a magic sound that modern makers can't reach just doesn't hold up once players can't see what they're holding. And honestly, I find that good news. It means a talented young violinist doesn't need a fortune to own an instrument that sounds excellent.

For Thursday, think about one more question. Could the same thing happen with other things we judge by their price, like food or paintings? Bring one example to class.
prompt: Why does the speaker mention what a single old violin can sell for?
choices: To argue that new violins today are sold for too much
To show how strongly people believed in the old violins
To explain why few players had ever touched the old violins
To explain why the room in the first test was kept dim
correct_answer: To show how strongly people believed in the old violins
